reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents an educational developer walkthrough for deploying an AI-agent identity and related contracts on Avalanche testnet. The private-key configuration and faucet interaction are described as operational setup steps, with viewers directed to use a wallet containing no real money and not share its key. the available video evidence does not describe a request for real funds or a financial product or investment opportunity.

citations.quote: In this video, I break down exactly what an AI Agent is and show you step-by-step how to deploy a live AI Agent Identity on the Avalanche blockchain using the new ERC-8004 standard.
Open vs code and terminal, clone the code from github, and, Install the dependencies, add your wallet private key and deploy it to avalanche
All coding demonstrations are performed on a test network (Avalanche Fuji) using test tokens that have zero real-world monetary value.
And important use a test wallet only. Zero real money in it. Private key is master key to your wallet. So anyone who has it owns it. So never share that with anyone

opening.argument: The video links an easy digital-asset acquisition to a concrete viewer workflow. Viewers are told to visit a faucet, select a network and token, connect a wallet or enter an address, use the coupon code “Avalanche Academy,” and request 2 testnet tokens. That is a direct reward-for-action pathway, presented alongside instructions to configure and deploy a blockchain project. The fact that the tokens are described as test tokens limits their monetary value, but it does not eliminate the solicitation pattern: the viewer is still directed to an external site, a wallet interaction, and a code-conditioned claim. The deployment step also requires entering a wallet private key into the project configuration, making the combined flow unusually sensitive for an allegedly simple tutorial.

citations.quote: to get the testnet tokens you have to visit the site then select the network the next select the token to receive and then you can connect your wallet here or you can type your address here.
And for the coupon code, you can write Avalanche Academy. And from here you can request 2 AVEX Testnet tokens.
Now to have private key, go to Account. Then click options... And here Show Private key... And this is your private key. Copy this.
Now go to vscode and in private key paste the wallet address but also remove the 0x from first and then save the file

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the faucet interaction operational setup does not change that the video directs viewers to claim tokens through an external site, wallet connection or address submission, and a coupon code. The disclaimer addresses monetary value, but the central action-for-asset structure remains. Likewise, warning viewers about private keys does not remove the risk created by instructing them to copy one into a project configuration before deployment.

citations.quote: you can connect your wallet here or you can type your address here.
And for the coupon code, you can write Avalanche Academy.
in private key paste the wallet address but also remove the 0x from first

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited steps do not promise a valuable reward or require payment. The video explicitly describes the tokens as testnet tokens, and the description says they have zero real-world monetary value. The private key is not requested from the audience or sent to the presenter; viewers are told to use a test wallet and not share it. Those facts make this a developer test flow, not a scam asset-acquisition scheme.

And important use a test wallet only. Zero real money in it.
So never share that with anyone

opening.argument: The video uses high-stakes crypto language to make deployment appear simple and immediately consequential. It says AI agents are handling real money, trading tokens, managing DeFi positions, and making financial decisions with “no human, no approval just code.” It then moves directly into cloning code, configuring a wallet private key, and running a deployment command. Even if the shown contract is described as an identity or tax agent, the presentation places that deployment inside a broader claim that autonomous agents can move real funds and produce serious financial effects. That combination of crypto credentials, automated financial activity, and a five-step deployment narrative can persuade viewers to treat a newly deployed contract as trustworthy before its behavior is independently established.

citations.quote: They're handling real money, trading tokens, managing DEFI positions all without any human in the loop.
AI agents are moving real money right now. No human, no approval just code.
Private key is master key to your wallet. So anyone who has it owns it
this is the moment one command npm run deploy fuji then enter

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference opening narrows the story to a testnet walkthrough, but the video's own framing repeatedly invokes real money, trading, DeFi, and autonomous financial decisions. The disclaimer does not erase those risk signals; it merely qualifies the particular demonstration. Nor does the warning about the private key answer why a novice should connect sensitive wallet configuration to a deployment presented as producing a permanent, verified agent identity.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The broad discussion of possible AI-agent applications is not a promise that this deployment generates profit, trades funds, or requires funding. The actual walkthrough uses a test wallet and testnet tokens, and the deployment command targets Fuji. The evidence therefore shows a developer demonstration surrounded by warnings, not a funded trading-bot or returns workflow.

one command npm run deploy fuji then enter

opening.argument: Although framed as education, the video actively steers viewers through participation in an external crypto ecosystem. It supplies a repository, a faucet workflow, a coupon code, wallet setup, private-key configuration, and a deployment command, then concludes that viewers have built a “verified on-chain agent identity” and invites them to continue through the video's links. The repeated claims that the system is permanent, public, and trustworthy give the operational instructions promotional force. A disclaimer saying the video is not promotional does not outweigh the concrete sequence that moves a viewer from watching to obtaining tokens, configuring a wallet, and deploying contracts.

And for the coupon code, you can write Avalanche Academy. And from here you can request 2 AVEX Testnet tokens.
then go to the terminal and this is the moment one command npm run deploy fuji then enter
Look at what you just built. A verified on-chain agent identity, a public reputation system, a validation layer, all live on avalanche

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference side calls this instruction, but instruction and promotion can coexist when the content directs viewers to a repository, faucet, coupon code, wallet setup, and deployment. The closing success framing encourages the viewer to regard the result as “verified” and “trustworthy,” while the actual evidence only shows that a deployment occurred on a test network. The disclaimer is a stated position, not proof that the presentation lacks promotional effect.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The operational details are consistent with a coding tutorial, not a solicitation for money or a paid product. The description expressly calls the material educational and says it does not endorse buying, selling, or trading digital assets. The result is demonstrated on Fuji with tokens that have no real-world monetary value, so promotional tone alone does not establish a scam.
